html:
The main square of Venice and, with the smaller Piazzetta that runs down to the water, the centre of its religious and political life. St Mark's Basilica closes the east end, and the Doge's Palace lines the Piazzetta. A remark often credited to Napoleon, without proof, called it "the drawing room of Europe".

In the 9th century there was only a small open space in front of the church, cut off by a stream. Doge Sebastiano Ziani (1172 to 1178) had the stream filled in, a church moved back and buildings bought and cleared, which gave the square its size; arcaded offices for the Procurators of St Mark lined its sides. The two granite columns on the Piazzetta, carrying the winged lion of Saint Mark and Saint Theodore, were raised about 1268, and executions took place between them. Spoils from the sack of Constantinople in 1204 were set up around the square, among them the so-called Pillars of Acre, which in fact came from a church in Constantinople.

The square took its present shape in the 16th century. The clock tower was finished in 1499. Jacopo Sansovino, who came to Venice after the sack of Rome in 1527, built the Library and the Loggetta from 1537 and had the south side moved back clear of the bell tower. Napoleon closed the west end with a new wing about 1810. The bell tower, built in the 12th century, collapsed on 14 July 1902 and was rebuilt "as it was, where it was" by 1912. The square lies low and floods at high tide, the acqua alta, as in the great flood of 1966.
